title: Firewalls and Network Security
description: Learn how firewalls protect networks and how security layers work together.

data.text: Network security is built in layers, and the firewall is the most visible gatekeeper. A firewall inspects traffic and decides whether to allow, block, or log each packet or connection. Modern security architectures combine traditional firewalls with web application firewalls, intrusion detection systems, and zero-trust policies to defend against increasingly sophisticated attacks.

Understanding firewalls is not just for security teams. Every backend engineer should know what ports and protocols their services use, how traffic flows through cloud security groups, and why certain requests are being blocked during a production incident.

data.title: Firewall Categories
items: Packet-filtering firewall — inspects source/destination IP, port, and protocol. Fast but limited.
Stateful inspection — tracks active connections and makes decisions based on connection state.
Proxy firewall — acts as an intermediary, terminating client connections and opening new ones to servers. Can inspect application data.
Next-generation firewall (NGFW) — combines stateful inspection with deep packet inspection, intrusion prevention, and application awareness.

data.text: A Web Application Firewall sits in front of your web server and inspects HTTP traffic for common attacks. WAFs look for SQL injection patterns, cross-site scripting attempts, path traversal, and other known exploits. They can block malicious requests before they ever reach your application code.

Popular WAFs include Cloudflare WAF, AWS WAF, and ModSecurity. Most can be deployed in minutes and come with pre-built rule sets maintained by security researchers. However, WAFs are not a silver bullet. They should complement, not replace, secure coding practices.

No single security layer catches everything. Defense in depth means overlapping controls so that if one fails, another catches the threat. A typical web application might combine a perimeter firewall, a WAF, TLS encryption, least-privilege IAM roles, database access controls, and application-layer validation.

data.caption: Layers of network and application security working together.

data.title: Common Firewall Mistakes
data.text: Overly permissive rules — such as 0.0.0.0/0 on database ports — are one of the most common cloud security issues. Always audit rules after changes, remove unused rules, and prefer allowlists over blocklists.

terms.definition: Traffic entering a network or resource, such as incoming HTTP requests.
Traffic leaving a network or resource. Modern firewalls also restrict outbound connections.
A security model that assumes no implicit trust. Every request is authenticated and authorized, regardless of where it originates.

data.title: AWS Security Group Example
data.content: Allow HTTPS from anywhere, SSH only from a corporate IP, and database access only from the app tier.
data.code:
# Allow inbound HTTPS from the internet
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-123456 \
  --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

# Allow inbound SSH from corporate network only
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-123456 \
  --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 203.0.113.0/24

# Allow database port from app tier security group
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-db789012 \
  --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group sg-app345678

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Firewalls enforce access control policies at network boundaries.
Layer 3/4 firewalls filter IPs and ports; WAFs inspect application-layer HTTP traffic.
Defense in depth combines multiple overlapping security layers.
Firewalls protect against external threats but must be configured precisely to avoid accidental lockouts or breaches.
data.takeaway: Effective network security is about layered controls, continuous auditing, and understanding what traffic your applications actually need.
